Compare

Ten agents. Archie is the only one that works on your own computer and asks your permission first, with no off switch.

Six work on a computer their company runs. Three work on yours, and on each of those, asking your permission is a setting you can turn off. Archie does both: calendar changes are confirmed, nothing is sent until you send it, and it stops before an order is final, and none of that is a setting.

Every placement and price on these pages is read from the other company’s own page and dated, and every page names where the other side wins.

Ten agents, two questions

Nine of the ten fail one of the two.

Every agent we could source

Ten agents, placed from what their own pages say.

The same ten on two axes, every placement quoted below. Across is where the work happens, on their servers or on your computer, and it is two answers rather than a scale. Up is your pick. Asks first is what a product does before a step that matters: it acts unless you set it to ask, it asks by default until you change a setting, or it asks every time and there is no setting. Ease is how you get it running: from a terminal, by downloading an app, or by signing in. The top right is the corner we are aiming at, and in the Ease view nobody has reached it, us included. Read September 18, 2026.

Where the other nine win

Five things they do that Archie does not.

Free, open source and on your computer

Hermes, OpenClaw and Vellum cost nothing to run, and their code is published, so you can read every line and write anything you can imagineSource 2Source 3Source 4. Archie’s is not, and a new ability is a new version from us. You can watch every connection it makes instead, and our proof page hands you the commands.

The most control on the board

OpenClaw has five permission modes, one that asks before every command, and allow lists per commandSource 3. On Archie, asking your permission is built in and has no off switch: less to set up, and less to change.

Working while everything you own is off

The six on their company’s computers keep going with your laptop shut. Archie works while your computer is awake, and what to leave on is on How It Works.

A free plan that renews every month

Muse and Symphony each have one, with the AI inside itSource 7Source 8. Archie is free on an AI account of your own, 20 jobs a day, and you pay that company for what you use.

A phone app of their own

Symphony, Muse and Vellum each ship oneSource 8Source 7Source 2. Archie reaches your phone through a chat app you connect, and Archie Mobile is in build.

Sources for every placement and claim on this page
1Archie: custody, what it asks, and how you get it

Our own Trust page, claim by claim, with the code behind each one: the work happens on your computer, on an AI account you own; calendar changes are confirmed, nothing is sent until you send it, and it stops before an order is final; and none of that is a setting you can turn off. Archie is a download from our install page, which is the app row.

2Vellum: runs locally by default, and asks until you change a setting

Read from vellum.ai on September 16, 2026. “By default, your assistant runs locally.” And: “High-stakes actions like sending emails to new contacts, modifying important files, or spending credits require explicit approval until you mark them as trusted.” Its permissions docs, read September 18, give four modes, from Strict, “Everything: every action requires explicit approval”, to Full access, “your assistant never asks for permission”, which is why asking your permission is a setting there. Its download page, read September 18, offers “Vellum for Mac: Native Mac app with computer use” and “Vellum for Windows: Desktop app for Windows PCs”, which is the app row. The page also says Vellum is open source and reaches “iOS, Android, web app, voice, email, Telegram, Slack, and terminal”, and its pricing page, read September 16, says “Vellum is free to download and start.”

3OpenClaw: on your machine, free, and acting on its own by default

Read from openclaw.ai on September 16, 2026. “Mac, Windows, or Linux. Bring hosted, subscription-backed, gateway, or local models. State lives on your machine, not a vendor cloud.” And: “No subscription. No hosted tier. No token.” It is MIT licensed. Its docs on tool and agent permissions, read the same day: “Full Access, including Default (Full Access), authorizes permitted changes without an approval prompt; restricted runs require human approval”, so by default it acts on its own, and you can make it ask. Read again September 18: its exec approvals give five modes, “deny”, “allowlist”, “ask”, “auto” and “full”, an “ask: always” that “keeps prompting”, and per-command allow lists, which is the most control on this board. Its getting-started is a shell command, “Try it in one command”, which is the terminal row; openclaw.ai also offers “Desktop Apps: Full apps that install everything for you”.

4Hermes: a desktop app, free and MIT, and asking by default

Read from hermes-agent.nousresearch.com on September 16, 2026, the Nous Research page for it. It offers a desktop app for macOS 12+, Windows 10/11 and Linux, and “Deploy to the cloud” through Nous Portal, and it is “free and open source under the MIT license”. Its security docs, read the same day: “Before executing any command, Hermes checks it against a curated list of dangerous patterns. If a match is found, the user must explicitly approve it”, with three modes, “smart | manual | off”, which is why asking your permission is a setting there. Its site leads with “Download desktop app”, which is the app row.

5Claude Cowork: Anthropic’s servers, and a mode that does not ask

Read from Anthropic’s own Cowork guide on August 20, 2026. “Open Claude on the web at claude.ai, in the Claude Desktop app, or in the Claude mobile app”, choose Cowork, and “describe the task you want Claude to complete”, which is the sign-in row. Cowork’s work “runs on Anthropic’s servers, in an isolated environment, and your sessions and files are saved to your Claude account”. Re-read September 16, 2026: the mode selector “offers Auto and Manual (default)”, in Manual “Claude pauses and asks for approval for actions”, and in Skip mode “Claude doesn’t pause to ask and nothing checks its actions automatically”.

6Grok Bot: a persistent cloud VM

Read from x.ai/news/introducing-grok-bot and the Grok Bot overview on August 20, 2026, and again September 16. Each Grok Bot “runs on a persistent cloud VM with a browser, filesystem, and terminal”, and “They finish jobs end to end, and only come back when something needs your approval”. The same page says “Download the app, create your first teammate, and start handing off work”, with a Download for macOS button, which is the app row.

7Meta Muse: a dedicated cloud computer, free for most

Read from Meta’s own announcement on September 15, 2026. Muse “runs on its own dedicated computer in the cloud, contained so no one else’s agent can reach it”, and is “free for most of what people need, with subscription plans for people who want to do more”. It is “rolling out in the US on iOS, Android, and muse.ai”, which is the sign-in row. Its permissions are one of two settings, “Always ask” or “Ask for some actions”, and Meta’s help centre, read the same day, says “By default, Muse will not take many important actions, like sending an email, without your approval.”

8Wix Symphony: how you reach it, and where the work happens

Read from wix.com/symphony on September 11, 2026. Symphony is used with a Wix account, in a browser or its iOS and Android apps, and Wix publishes no program you run on your own computer, which is the sign-in row. Wix’s own overview says it “checks with you first before your agents act, so nothing important happens without your approval”. Read again September 18: “Your agents connect to the suite of tools you already use and can work on their own, 24/7”, and “your agents’ background work uses AI credits”. Wix publishes no sentence saying where that work runs. Work that goes on while you are away, on a product that ships only a phone app and a browser, is not happening on a computer of yours, and that is why Symphony sits on the their-servers side: it is our reading of those two sentences, not a quote, and if Wix publishes the sentence either way we will cite it. Its pricing page, read September 11: a free plan, “no credit card needed”, whose credits “reset monthly”.

9Instinct: in private access, hosted, and acting on its own

Read from instinct.com on September 16, 2026. “Text Instinct to get started”: nothing is installed, which is the sign-in row, and it is “currently available to a private access group as we’re scaling up compute”. Its privacy policy, read the same day, places it: the service is provided with “third-party hosting”, and its features “can perform tasks or take actions independently on your behalf, based on the permissions you grant”.

10Norton Family Assistant: asks first, and runs in the cloud

Read from us.norton.com/products/family-assistant on September 16, 2026: “Asks first, acts after”. Its support FAQ, read September 18, 2026, says where it runs: “your family graph, connected-account tokens, agent context, and chat history all live inside your own dedicated instance in the cloud, isolated from other users”, which is why it sits on the their-servers side. It “works on any PCs that run in browsers such as Norton Neo, Chrome, and Firefox” or as an iPhone app, which is the sign-in row.
